title: Opstandingskerk (Kolenkit)
summary: The 1956 church whose coal-scuttle bell tower gave the whole Kolenkitbuurt its name, with a neighbourhood centre built into its basement.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Sint-Josephkerk
summary: One of the first Dutch Catholic churches built entirely in exposed concrete, inspired by Perret and Le Corbusier. Since 2016 it has been an indoor children's playground.
body:
G.H.M. Holt designed this church in 1941-1943, working with K.P. Tholens. It was built in 1950-1952 and consecrated on 22 May 1952. It is one of the first Catholic churches in the Netherlands built wholly in concrete, with the concrete frame left visible, at a time when conservative Catholics doubted the material. Holt drew on the concrete churches of the Perret brothers and Le Corbusier.

From the square, look at the open concrete atrium in front of the entrance, the broad tower with its open bell frame and concrete louvres, and the octagonal baptistery with a tapering lantern studded with round glass blocks. The yellowish concrete panels on the nave were made to recall Bentheim sandstone. The low aisles are filled in with Limburg rubble stone.

The adjoining convent, pastorie and sacristy at Robert Scottstraat 7 (Holt and Tholens, 1952-1953) are a separate municipal monument. They mix sober traditionalism with very early brutalism and have an unusually high plinth of multicoloured stone. The church closed for worship in 1990. It then served as a climbing hall (1996-2012) and as the squatted 'Vluchtkerk' for refused asylum seekers (2012-2013). It reopened in 2016 as a children's play centre, and the ceiling painting by Marius de Leeuw has been restored.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: De Boom (Boomkerk)
summary: A neo-Romanesque church of 1911 that replaced a clandestine church on the Kalverstraat and still houses its 1774 Hilgers organ.
body:
The Franciscan parish of 't Boompje had worshipped since the 16th century in a clandestine church on the Kalverstraat. The site was sold to the department store Vroom & Dreesmann, and the money paid for this church, then in the municipality of Sloten. P.J. Bekkers, trained in the circle of P.J.H. Cuypers, designed it in 1910, and it was consecrated on 7 May 1911.

Look for the tall corner tower with its blind arches and dwarf gallery, the rose window above three round-arched portals with tiled angels in their gables, and statues of Mary, Francis of Assisi and Anthony of Padua on the facade. Inside are statues, paintings, altars and the 1774 organ by Johannes Petrus Hilgers, all brought from the old church. The organ is used for concerts again since the 2013-2015 restoration.

The pastorie at no. 408 was built at the same time by Bekkers but in a different style. Its symmetrical, villa-like front is inspired by 18th-century classicism, with a metal tree from the old clandestine church above the door. A corridor links it to the church. Franciscans lived there until 1985. The church sits slightly back from today's building line, a trace of the pre-urban road layout. It is now the central Catholic church of Amsterdam-West.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Koningsvrouwen van Landlust
summary: Among the first rows of strokenbouw in Amsterdam: 1930s Nieuwe Bouwen housing by Merkelbach & Karsten and G. Versteeg, laid out in parallel rows instead of closed blocks.
body:
Landlust was one of the first plans in which Cornelis van Eesteren's department of urban development tried out modern town planning. In 1933 the plan was changed. Between the Juliana van Stolbergstraat and the Karel Doormanstraat, the closed perimeter blocks were replaced by *strokenbouw*: parallel rows of flats with open green strips between them, so every home got the same sun and air. It was one of the first strokenbouw projects in the country, and an early example of the open building pattern later used across western Amsterdam.

The two protected complexes are housing in the Nieuwe Bouwen style. The part designed by Ben Merkelbach and Charles Karsten runs along the Juliana van Stolbergstraat and Louise de Colignystraat (even numbers), Bestevâerstraat 232-238 and Willem de Zwijgerlaan 331. G. Versteeg designed the part along the Charlotte de Bourbonstraat and the odd side of the Louise de Colignystraat, Bestevâerstraat 220-230 and Willem de Zwijgerlaan 329. The flats were built in the mid- to late 1930s; sources give dates between 1933 and 1938.

The nickname refers to the street names. Charlotte de Bourbon and Louise de Coligny were wives of William of Orange, and Juliana van Stolberg was his mother. Walk the rows to see the repetitive, flat-roofed blocks and the green spaces between them.

attributes.architect: Ben Merkelbach and Charles Karsten; G. Versteeg

note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Keesmanblokken and Gibraltarbadje
summary: Three gently curving post-war blocks of flats around lawns and a public paddling pool. The city calls the layout unique in Amsterdam.
body:
This site was meant for a cluster of schools. After the 1933 education cuts, the plan was changed in 1940 to housing, and Cornelis Keesman built the complex in 1946-1949. It has three north-south blocks of five storeys. The two outer blocks curve slightly, and the middle one is set 20 metres further south. Low two-storey blocks for older people close off the south ends. Two of the streets inside the complex are dead ends, which keeps the green space safe for children.

Things to notice: the ground-floor storage galleries carried on octagonal columns, the half-recessed balconies and narrow bay windows on the west side, the projecting and upturned roof edge, the granite stairwells visible through the tall stairwell windows, and the rounded touches such as the curved front of the former boiler house.

At the north end, where the blocks meet the Gibraltarstraat, is the **Gibraltarbadje**, a public paddling pool designed by J.H. (Ko) Mulder of Public Works and opened in 1952. It is lined with pale blue tiles. A bronze fountain figure of a woman with a jug by Gerrit Bolhuis (1950) stands at the edge, and a blue sea lion and octopus were added later. The pool is protected as part of this monument. It is open to the public in summer.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Jan van Galenbrug (Brug 382)
summary: Piet Kramer's Amsterdam School bascule bridge of 1935, covered in sculpture: gabled warehouses with porters, cranes, sea lions, Jonah and the whale, and a sea monster.

title: Vierwindstrekenbrug
summary: A Piet Kramer bridge from the early 1930s whose four corner sculptures by Hildo Krop show the four points of the compass as seen from 1930s Amsterdam.

title: De Bloem (De Blom)
summary: An 18th-century corn mill that stood on the city ramparts until 1877 and was rebuilt here on the Haarlemmerweg in 1878.
body:
This *stellingmolen*, an octagonal smock mill with a raised stage around the body, dates from 1768. It first stood on the Rijkeroort bastion at the end of the Bloemgracht, and the old name of that bastion, De Blom, gave both the mill and the canal their names. When the Marnixstraat was laid out, the mill was taken down in 1877 and rebuilt in 1878 on this spot, then in the municipality of Sloten. It got a four-metre brick base below the octagonal body. Locals also call it the '400 Roe' mill, after its distance of 400 rods from the Haarlemmerpoort.

The city bought it in 1927. Under the Schuurman firm it got an electric mill so it could grind on windless days, and it worked commercially until 1960. A spice trader, Schuurmans Specerijen, used it from 1967 to 1998. It still has three pairs of wind-driven millstones and two attached houses. Volunteers keep it running as a corn mill. It is usually closed to visitors but sometimes opens on special days. From the Haarlemmerweg you can see the sails, the brick base and the stage. In the early hours of New Year's Day 2014 it was damaged by fire, probably caused by fireworks.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Wijdeveld's stadspoort (north block)
summary: The northern half of H.Th. Wijdeveld's 1920s 'city gate' at Hoofdweg and Jan van Galenstraat, a six-storey tower block with former artists' studios at the top.
body:
Where the Hoofdweg crosses the Jan van Galenstraat, architect H.Th. Wijdeveld framed the junction as a *stadspoort*, a city gate, as part of the Hoofdweg housing in Amsterdam's Plan-West. This rijksmonument is the northern corner block, built in 1925-1926 with workers' housing, shops, and studio flats on the top floors.

Look for the slightly set-back rectangular tower of six storeys rising higher at the back. It has large three-part windows and a many-paned glass front where the studios were. Along the Jan van Galenstraat, the ground and first floors project and end in a half-round bay. Above the shopfronts there is a band of decorative brickwork with vertical accents, then a projecting row of tall triple windows. The high blind wall of the attic storey has four hoisting beams with square elements above. A narrow projecting section with slim windows makes the transition to the neighbouring Hoofdweg houses.

The register values the block for its typology and its role in the ensemble. It is best read together with the opposite corner, which completes the gate.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: GAK-gebouw
summary: Ben Merkelbach's last building: when it opened in 1960 this glass-walled office by the A10 was one of the largest and most modern in the Netherlands. It is now housing.
body:
Built for the Gemeenschappelijk Administratiekantoor (GAK), the national social-insurance administration office, this vast office opened in 1960. It was one of the largest and most modern office buildings in the Netherlands. It was the last project of Ben Merkelbach, Amsterdam's city architect from 1956 to 1961, designed with P.J. Elling, and a high point of his functionalist work. The city calls it a monument of post-war social legislation and social democracy.

The layout of a plinth, a central block and long office wings is still easy to read. The striking curtain walls were redesigned but keep the original look, which earned it the local nickname 'Aquarium'. Standing right by the ring road, it is a landmark for the whole neighbourhood.

The building has been split into three separate units and largely converted to housing (around 2012). The original interior 'squares', 'villages' and 'streets' are gone. Only the stairs in the emergency stairwells survive. Outside, look for the sculpture gallery with pergola and pond, and the two works by Carel Visser made for this spot: *2 U's naar buiten, 2 U's naar binnen* and *Watertafel*.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Zaanstad (Elseviergebouw)
summary: A late work by Willem Dudok: a 40-metre office slab of the 1960s that towers over low housing and has been converted into apartments.
body:
Willem Marinus Dudok, best known for Hilversum town hall, designed this office block with Robert Magnée after he had retired. It was built from 1964 to 1967. Officially called West-Kantoor, it took the nickname 'Elseviergebouw' from its best-known tenant, Reed Elsevier, which stayed until 2005. The architects wanted 18 storeys, but the city allowed only twelve, about 40 metres. That is still far taller than the surrounding four- and five-storey housing, so the building dominates the area.

The city values it as a careful functionalist design and a representative example of Dudok's post-war work. Unlike his earlier, more picturesque buildings, he aimed here for unity and clear main volumes. In 2012-2015 it was converted into studios, apartments and penthouses, now under the name Zaanstad. The exterior was renovated with the original articulation kept. The entrance moved to the Krelis Louwenstraat, the end wall got windows and balconies, and the ring-road side got noise insulation. It became a municipal monument on 25 June 2019.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Prinses Beatrixschool (Multatulischool)
summary: The very first of Amsterdam's post-war 'H-schools', light-and-air primary schools descended from Duiker's open-air school. Still in near-original condition.
body:
Opened on 14 April 1953, this was the first of a new series of permanent schools by the city's Public Works department, designed under its chief architect Jan Leupen. The type grew out of a post-war drive for healthy schools after tuberculosis deaths rose again in 1945. It follows on from Jan Duiker's Open-Air School of 1930. Two parallel buildings, one for classrooms and one for the gym, assembly hall and craft rooms, are joined by two low glazed corridors, giving an H-shaped plan with playgrounds in the gaps. Classrooms have no corridors and windows on both sides for daylight and cross-ventilation.

From the street, look for the classroom windows grouped in threes with white frames and coloured panels below, and the tall 'ladder' windows of the stairwells running up to the roof ridge. Inside there is a real stage hall, and in 1956 Theo Kurpershoek made four inlaid brick-and-mosaic murals of the four elements in the break hall. Queen Juliana visited in 1953. Now the Multatulischool, it is described as the best-preserved of its kind. A sandpit by Aldo van Eyck is on the grounds. It is part of the 'Scholendriehoek', with three more listed schools next door.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Prinses Margrietschool
summary: The first of Amsterdam's permanent post-war nursery schools: red brick, big windows on both sides of every classroom, and Limburg marl stone running from the porch into the hall.
body:
Built in 1953 by the Public Works department as the nursery-school partner of the Prinses Beatrixschool next door, this was the first of a new series of permanent kindergartens. Wikipedia names Kees van der Wilk as the architect. Like the H-schools, it has no corridors: classrooms connect directly, so each has large windows on two sides for light and fresh air.

The symmetrical two-storey building has red brick walls and a low pitched roof. Look at the front: the stepped wings, the pergola over the central entrance and the walls of Limburg marl stone, which continue into the glazed hall. The city's description links this blurred inside-outside threshold to ideas later made famous by the magazine *Forum* and Aldo van Eyck. The classroom windows are white timber grids with tilting lower sashes, once painted in a contrasting colour.

The interior is described as entirely original, with red tiles, teak floors and the original classroom doors. A bronze of a girl with a ponytail, once in the playground, now stands in the hall. An Aldo van Eyck climbing frame stands in the playground. The building serves as an annex of the Multatulischool.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Daniël Goedkoopschool
summary: Amsterdam's first post-war ULO school (1960), by Manon Peyrot, one of very few women architects at the city's Public Works department.
body:
The third school on the 'Scholendriehoek' opened mid-year on 4 February 1960 as the city's first post-war ULO, a school for extended primary education. Its designer, Manon Peyrot, worked at the Public Works department when a woman in that role was far from usual, and the city gives the building cultural value for that alone.

The city describes four wings around a courtyard, reached by stairwells instead of corridors. A steel-and-glass bridge links two of the wings, and the design reads as a variant of the H-schools next door. The ground floor held bike storage, changing rooms and cloakrooms, with classrooms, gym and stage hall above, all lit by large areas of glass. The low pavilion-like building on its lawn contrasts with the housing around it. As far as the city knows, it is the only surviving school of its type in Amsterdam.

The sober, functionalist exterior is largely original. The interior has been changed, and the original mural and bronze sculpture are gone. Since 2013 the owner, Stichting Witboek, has used it for social, cultural and educational activities for local residents.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Hendrick de Keyserschool
summary: A large modernist technical school of 1960 by Arno Nicolaï, with concrete reliefs and murals by Lex Horn. When it was listed, its interior was almost untouched down to the lamps and colours.
body:
Arno Nicolaï, Prix de Rome winner and later known for Emmerhout in Emmen, designed this Uitgebreide Technische School in 1960, across the street from the Scholendriehoek. Five linked blocks of different heights are grouped around a courtyard. The longest, on the Wiltzanghlaan, has five storeys of south-facing classrooms, which makes it a landmark in the area.

The concrete frame is visible everywhere and filled in with ribbed concrete parapets, steel windows and ribbed red brick. The original colours are pale grey, white and faded blue. Iron letters over the entrance read HENDRICK DE KEIJSERSCHOOL. On the projecting assembly-hall block there is a concrete relief of abstracted human figures by Lex Horn. Horn also painted the hall mural of tradesmen with Icarus and an aeroplane. His many commissions came partly from the 1% arts rule for schools that he had helped bring about.

When the city described it, the interior was remarkably complete, with the aisled assembly hall, stage, linoleum, lamps, timetable boards and even toilets. The school had closed by then, and parts were used as artists' studios.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: De Kamperfoelie
summary: A white timber-and-glass kindergarten of 1949 with a Mondrian-like grid of windows, the last survivor of Amsterdam's first series of 'semi-permanent' post-war nursery schools.
body:
Built in 1949 by the Public Works department, this two-storey kindergarten stands back from the brick housing walls of the Kijkduinstraat, at a bend in the street. It is a light, timber-framed building on a concrete base, designed in the spirit of the Nieuwe Bouwen. Behind its front building, a covered corridor leads to a rear wing of garden classrooms with doors opening onto the garden. Most rooms have windows on two facing sides, a semi-open-air approach meant to give children plenty of light and air at a time of renewed fear of tuberculosis.

The facade is a grid of rectangular modules: glazed for classrooms, closed with aluminium panels for service rooms, and all framed in white. The city compares the effect to a Mondrian painting. Some panels are now painted white and blue. The rear facade lost its original three-module grid in a renovation.

Similar schools at the Hertspiegelweg and elsewhere were demolished, so this is the last of the earliest series. Its plan of front building, rear building and connecting corridor follows Amsterdam schools of the 1920s and 30s. The school closed in the early 1980s, and the building was later used by local services and small organisations.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Sint Hubertusschool
summary: A Catholic bakers' and catering school of the late 1950s by Evers & Sarlemijn, a stately example of the Bossche School with a column of Saint Hubert by Niel Steenbergen at the entrance.
body:
Aart Evers and Geert Sarlemijn, leading Amsterdam architects of the Bossche School, designed this building as the Catholic bakers', confectioners' and catering school Sint Hubertus. It was completed in the late 1950s; the city gives 1957 and Wikipedia gives 1959-1960. The Bossche School grew out of Dom Hans van der Laan's courses in 's-Hertogenbosch from 1947. It worked with classical proportions, sober volumes and brickwork with coarse joints.

The yellow brick block, laid in a random bond, seems to float above a recessed concrete plinth. A recessed entrance to the left of centre, reached by a gravel-concrete terrace and steps, is framed almost like an Italian palazzo. It lines up with the view down the Merlijnstraat. Look for the polygonal concrete columns of the top-floor loggias at both ends. Inside, two stacked halls with a gallery, meander patterns on the ceilings and linoleum, and the corridors and stairwells largely survived a 2003 renovation.

On the entrance terrace stands Niel Steenbergen's limestone column topped by Saint Hubert, patron of hunters and of the 'Hubertus rolls'. Its reliefs tell his story, like a small Trajan's Column. Baking courses stayed here until 2015. Since 2019 the building has housed a secondary school.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Robert Scottstraat 28 (De Springplank)
summary: A 1954 double primary school on concrete pilotis by Tholens and Van Steenhardt Carré, restored in 2013 with its original colours and artworks back on view.
body:
Built in 1954 between two blocks of brick walk-up flats, this school was designed by K.P. Tholens and L. van Steenhardt Carré as a double Catholic school, with the Juliaschool for girls and the Sint-Franciscusschool for boys. Its functionalist design stands out from the housing around it. The visible concrete frame is filled with brick or large windows, and on the ground floor the upper storeys rest on concrete columns (pilotis), so the long three-storey block seems to float. The stairwells are at the back, on the playground side.

It is a corridor school with a gym on the ground floor, designed for plenty of light, air and space. The city notes several works of monumental art inside. A careful 2013 renovation kept the structure, restored the original colours and put all the art back on display.

The school belongs to the Catholic ensemble around the Sint-Josephkerk, with the church, convent, old people's housing and other schools, which forms the heart of this neighbourhood. Today it houses basisschool De Springplank and a branch of a ballet school.

attributes.architect: L. van Steenhardt Carré and K.P. Tholens

note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Former ULO school, Erik de Roodestraat 18
summary: A Bossche School secondary school by Evers & Sarlemijn with a Roman-style atrium hall, a courtyard fountain with a bronze by A. Teeuwisse and a painted ceiling by Caveto.
body:
This former ULO school, commissioned by the Broeders van Maastricht, is part of the Catholic ensemble around the Sint-Josephkerk: church, old people's homes, kindergarten and the Franciscus- and Juliaschool. Together they form the centre of the neighbourhood. The ensemble's plans of 1934 and 1944 show the post-war shift towards the idea of a neighbourhood centre.

A. Evers and G.J.M. Sarlemijn, among the leading architects of the Bossche School, designed it in 1954. The style looked to classical proportions, and here that goes further than usual. The entrance hall is laid out as an atrium and opens onto a courtyard with a fountain, which the city links directly to classical Roman architecture. Both the main form and the details are well preserved.

The art was made for the building: a bronze sculpture by A. Teeuwisse in the courtyard fountain, and a ceiling in the school hall painted by Caveto (J.J.M. Dohmen). From the street you mainly see the sober, carefully proportioned brick volume. The atrium and courtyard are inside.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Pniëlkerk ('het Theelichtje')
summary: A white Reformed church of the 1950s whose concrete walls, pierced with glass tiles, glow like a tealight. It is now the Podium Mozaïek theatre.
body:
B.T. Boeyinga, who shaped the Gereformeerd (Reformed) church building in the Netherlands, designed this church as his last major work. A 1945 design in the traditional Delft School style was dropped. The building that went up in 1954-1955 is almost businesslike, free-standing and sitting comfortably among the early strokenbouw around it. Two slender bell towers with steel tops give it a modest vertical accent.

The walls are made of square concrete elements set on their points. Some are solid. Others are pierced with glass tiles in a geometric pattern and grouped into wide bands that act as the windows. Lit from inside, the church looks like a tealight, hence the nickname *het Theelichtje*. It is also called De Witte Kerk. Inside, the pulpit stood where three sightlines crossed, a type Boeyinga developed for Reformed worship. The hall at the back has a floating steel stair and a gallery on concrete yokes that recall Jan Duiker.

Since 2005 the building has been the theatre Podium Mozaïek, together with a GP practice, so you can see the interior by going to a show. A new auditorium was built into the church hall, and the pulpit and one of Johan van den Broek's sandblasted glass reliefs were lost. The exterior was kept. The quiet square on the south side is worth a look.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Former Wereldbibliotheek
summary: The 1922 printing works and offices of the Wereldbibliotheek, the publisher of good, cheap books for working people. It is an expressive brick building close to the Amsterdam School.
body:
The Wereldbibliotheek was founded in 1905 by Leo Simons to publish good literature at low prices. That was a project of social uplift for working people, and the same Simons had commissioned Berlage to design his house. In 1922 the firm moved into this building by L. Zwiers, a designer, illustrator and author from Berlage's circle. It held offices, a warehouse, a printing works and a bindery. The publisher stayed until 1976.

The long symmetrical front of red-grey brick has rounded corners and bands of tar-soaked dark brick that meander under the upper windows. The roof edge swells upward at the centre and at the ends. The projecting entrance porch, with two squat column-like piers, originally carried 'WERELD BIBLIOTHEEK' in wrought iron. At the entrance, the glass door, blue tile mosaic, coloured 'dripstone' glass ornaments and a stone letterbox marked 'post' are original.

The building is now divided among several businesses. The original canary-yellow window frames have been replaced, and the factory hall at the back is a patchwork of additions, so the city has called for careful restoration. Angled to the Haarlemmerweg, it closes off the Admiraal De Ruijterweg.
note: Imported from the City of Amsterdam monuments register, Wikidata and the Rijksmonumentenregister

title: Former post office, Admiraal De Ruijterweg
summary: One of the last buildings left from the village of Sloterdijk south of the Haarlemmerweg: a small 1910s post office with restrained Amsterdam School brickwork and its original stone letterbox.
